The belief: a LINQ query on a
is a database read. Run it again and you get whatever the row holds now, just like running the same

It's an easy thing to believe, because half of it is true. The query really does go to the database every time, and the log proves it. Most code never sees the other half: in ASP.NET Core a context lives for one request, so almost every query is the first one that context runs for that row. And
is usually presented as a performance switch, so tracking looks like a speed detail rather than something that changes what your query returns.
The missing half: EF Core runs the query, then decides for each row whether to use it at all.
The query runs, and the values are discarded
By default, a query that returns entity types is a tracking query. Every entity it returns is recorded in the context's
with a snapshot of its original values, so

can work out what you changed. When a later tracking query returns a row, EF Core checks its key first. If an instance with that key is already tracked, EF Core returns that instance and doesn't overwrite its current or original values with the row it just read. This is
: a context holds at most one instance per key.

Why EF Core works this way

It's deliberate. If a query overwrote tracked values, it would silently wipe out changes you've made but not saved, and two objects with the same key could disagree about their properties and relationships. One instance per key gives
a graph with no ambiguity. The price is that a context's picture of an entity is frozen at the moment it started tracking it. That's why Microsoft designs
: create it, load, change, save, dispose.
Where it bites: contexts that live too long
A scoped context in a web request rarely shows the problem. It shows up when a context outlives one operation: a

that resolves it once before its loop, a singleton holding one (the captive dependency problem), a Blazor Server component, where the scope lasts as long as the user's circuit, a desktop app, or a test that seeds and asserts through the same context.
